title: The Union's preacher, buried at Geary

place.label: Sarcophagus of Thomas Starr King, First Unitarian Church, 1187 Franklin Street at Geary

hook: One of the few graves San Francisco never moved belongs to the preacher who campaigned for the Union and raised a fortune for wounded soldiers.
story: Thomas Starr King came west in 1860 to lead First Unitarian, then a congregation deep in debt on Stockton Street. He cleared the debt and raised money for a larger church at 133 Geary Street near Union Square, finished by January 1864 [1]. When the Civil War began he toured California speaking for the Union and campaigned with his friend Leland Stanford. Lincoln allegedly credited him with keeping California in the Union [1]. He also raised more than $1.5 million for the U.S. Sanitary Commission. His plaque calls it the forerunner of the American Red Cross [1][2]. Worn out by constant travel, he died of diphtheria and pneumonia on 4 March 1864, aged 39. Around 20,000 people attended his funeral, and Bret Harte gave a eulogy [1]. He was entombed in a sarcophagus beside the church. In 1889 the congregation moved to Percy & Hamilton's rough granite Romanesque church at Franklin and Geary, and the tomb moved with it [1][3]. Most of the city's burials were later removed, but his sarcophagus still sits in the corner of the lot near O'Farrell Street [1].

title: A German church a block from dynamite

place.label: St. Mark's Lutheran Church, 1135 O'Farrell Street at Franklin

hook: In 1906 soldiers blew up buildings a block away and its cross melted in the heat. St. Mark's survived, and it took in the homeless.
story:
St. Mark's dates its founding to 1849, when German immigrants were arriving in Gold Rush San Francisco [1]. The congregation dedicated this church on Cathedral Hill on 10 March 1895. It was designed by the German-American architect Henry Geilfuss in a mix of Romanesque and Gothic styles [1][2]. The city's landmark listing calls it the oldest Lutheran church in the West [2].

The 1906 earthquake weakened the east tower. Then the fire came west. Dynamite was set off a block away, at O'Farrell and Van Ness, to make a firebreak. The heat of the fire was fierce enough to melt the church's cross [1]. The landmark record credits the Van Ness dynamiting with saving the building [2]. The fire stopped just short of the church, and St. Mark's immediately became a refuge for families left homeless by the disaster [1].

The church's Victorian neighbours did not last. Decades later redevelopment cleared hundreds of Western Addition homes, and the round Carillon Tower apartments rose behind it [2]. The 1895 church is still there.

title: Praying in masks on Van Ness

place.label: Site of the second St. Mary's Cathedral, Van Ness Avenue at O'Farrell Street (NW corner)

hook: In the autumn of 1918 San Francisco made masks the law, and worshippers gathered outdoors at the cathedral on Van Ness.
story:
Archbishop Patrick Riordan bought the corner of Van Ness Avenue and O'Farrell Street in 1883. He broke ground in 1885 and dedicated the new St. Mary's Cathedral in January 1891 [1]. Twenty-seven years later it faced a different kind of emergency.

The city's first case of Spanish flu was diagnosed on 23 September 1918 [2]. From 18 October the Board of Health closed theatres, schools and lodge meetings. According to the University of Michigan's influenza archive, it did not close churches but advised that services stop or be held in the open air [3]. A local account says churches were ordered shut, so the sources disagree [2]. From 25 October a city ordinance required everyone in public to wear a mask. On 27 October alone, police arrested 110 people for not wearing one [3].

A photograph from 1918 shows an outdoor service at the cathedral, with some worshippers in influenza masks [2]. By the time the epidemic ended in early 1919, the city had recorded almost 45,000 cases and more than 3,000 deaths [2]. The cathedral burned in 1962 and was replaced by the present cathedral on Cathedral Hill, completed in 1970 [1].

title: The heiress, the silver king and the brother

place.label: Theodore F. Payne House, 1409 Sutter Street between Franklin and Gough

hook: A Comstock millionaire died, a supposedly dead brother turned up to claim his share, and the niece's windfall helped build this turreted house.
story:
Theodore Payne reached San Francisco in 1849 with nothing. He had lost everything when his steamship sank before it arrived [1]. His son Theodore F. Payne married Mary Pauline O'Brien, whose unmarried uncle, William S. O'Brien, was one of the Comstock 'Silver Kings'. In 1877 O'Brien heard that his brother Patrick had died and left a wife and daughter destitute. He brought them west from Brooklyn [1]. O'Brien himself died on 2 May 1878, and news of his death was published all over the country. Then Patrick, very much alive, appeared to claim a share. To prevent a lawsuit over the will, the other heirs paid father and daughter over $600,000. With the $800,000 O'Brien had left her, Mary Pauline received more than twice as much as any other heir [1].

William Curlett designed the house, finished around 1881. It has an octagonal turret and about 16,000 square feet across four floors. The bathrooms were built into the house rather than added onto a porch, and the tubs and basins had hot and cold running water [1][2]. It is the last of the large houses that once lined this block of Sutter [2].

title: A house jacked up twelve feet

place.label: Goodman Building (St. Beryl Hotel), 1117 Geary Street between Van Ness and Franklin

hook: Seven weeks after the fire, a ladies' tailor filed plans to lift his 1869 house into the air and slide five shops underneath.
story:
In 1869 Joseph Emeric, a French immigrant who had become a Contra Costa landowner and a wine importer, built a residence on the south side of Geary between Van Ness and Franklin. The arched window heads still carry the letter 'E' [1]. His son Henry, a state assemblyman, served as State Fish Commissioner in the 1890s [1]. After Henry's death his daughter sold the building to Abraham and Sarah Goodman, New Yorkers who ran a ladies' tailoring business. The Register nomination dates the sale to 28 December 1900; the city landmark summary says 1899 [1][2].

The fire of 1906 destroyed everything east of the building, from Van Ness to the waterfront [1]. On 6 June 1906 Goodman applied for a permit to raise the two-storey frame building 12 feet and put five stores underneath. His architect, Conrad Meussdorffer, turned the upper floors into a hotel and added a mansard fourth floor as a photographer's studio for H. Pierre Smith [1]. The St. Beryl Hotel was named after Beryl Goodfriend, its first proprietress. The couple's son Mervin put the cost at about $50,000. It was one small answer to the housing shortage after the fire [1].

title: He sold to miners instead of digging

place.label: Stadtmuller House, 819 Eddy Street between Van Ness and Franklin

hook: A Nevada storekeeper made his money selling to silver miners, then built one of Eddy Street's showpiece Italianates.
story:
Frederick D. Stadtmuller made his money in Silver City, Nevada. He owned a chain of stores there, Stadtmuller & Co., and a timber business [1]. As NoeHill puts it, he sold things to the miners 'rather than grubbing around in the dirt' [2]. He moved to San Francisco in 1879 and went into California wines and brandies with the firm of Walter, Schilling & Co. One of his partners was Claus Schilling, brother of the spice maker A. Schilling [1].

In 1880 the architect P. R. Schmidt designed him this Italianate house on Eddy Street. It has two-storey bay windows, carved and panelled entrance doors, and a portico on fluted Corinthian columns under a carved balustrade [1]. The street was then a prosperous one [2]. The family kept the house until 1951. It then became a rooming house, as many large old homes did [1][2]. In 1963 Mr. and Mrs. Peter R. Loebs bought it and restored it as a single-family home. They kept its original woodwork and onyx and marble fireplaces [1].

title: Great is Ross the architect

place.label: Site of the Albert Pike Memorial Scottish Rite Temple, 1859 Geary Boulevard

hook: The Freemasons' temple on Geary was the work of a Scottish architect who once carved his own praise over a doorway.
story:
In May 1904 the Chronicle printed a sketch of a proposed Masonic temple for the south side of Geary between Fillmore and Steiner. It was to be three storeys of yellow brick and terra cotta in a Romanesque Revival style, valued at $80,000. The building appears on the 1905 Sanborn fire-insurance map [1]. It was named the Albert Pike Memorial Scottish Rite Temple, after the lawyer, writer, soldier and famous Freemason Albert Pike [1].

Its architect was Thomas Ross, a Scot who came to the United States in 1883. He also designed the Sing Fat and Sing Chong buildings at California and Grant, which are credited with inspiring Chinatown's pagoda-style rebuilding after 1906 [1]. For the Shriners on Geary near Jones he built a Moorish temple, now the Alcazar Theater. According to Bridget Maley, writing in The New Fillmore, he placed an Arabic inscription over its entry: 'Great is Allah and Great is Ross the Architect' [1][2].

The 1906 earthquake left the Geary temple structurally damaged, and it was repaired. The Masons used it until the mid-1960s. In the 1970s it became the San Francisco home of Jim Jones's Peoples Temple [1].

title: A temple finished twice

place.label: Site of Congregation Beth Israel's Geary Street Temple, 1839 Geary Boulevard

hook: The new synagogue was meant to open for the Jewish New Year of 1906. The earthquake came first.
story:
Congregation Beth Israel was founded in 1860. It worshipped on Sutter and Mission streets, then built synagogues on Turk Street in 1879 and on Geary near Octavia in 1891 [1][2]. In December 1905 it laid the cornerstone of a third temple at 1839 Geary. William Curlett designed it in a 'Byzantine style' to seat 1,600 at a cost of about $120,000, and it was due to open for the New Year beginning 19 September 1906 [2]. The earthquake of 18 April struck while it was still unfinished and badly damaged it [2][3]. The congregation rebuilt and dedicated the temple in 1908 [1][3]. Rabbi Meyer Solomon Levy led it until 1916, and Cantor Joseph Rabinowitz sang there from 1891 to 1943 [1].

The fire also sent Jewish families from South of Market into the Fillmore [4]. Jerry Flamm, writing about the 1920s Fillmore, described crowds outside the neighbourhood's three synagogues all day on the High Holidays. Some people could not afford membership. Others were non-believers who still wanted to 'be counted' [4]. Around the corner at 1740 O'Farrell, the Labor Lyceum's basement rooms were home to the Workmen's Circle and the Socialist Party [4]. A post office now stands on the temple's site [3].

title: The people's railroad rolls down Geary

place.label: Geary Street between Laguna and Webster, on the original Municipal Railway line

hook: After a bribery scandal and a bloody strike, voters bought a streetcar line of their own. Mayor Rolph took the controls on its first run.
story:
By 1902 one company, United Railroads, controlled nearly all of San Francisco's streetcar lines. In 1907 the graft prosecution revealed that the company had paid to secure the supervisors' consent. The same year it violently broke the carmen's strike, which earned it the lasting hostility of organized labour [1]. In December 1909, after three failed attempts, voters approved bonds by a three-to-one margin to buy the independent Geary Street cable line, electrify it and extend it down Market Street [1][2]. The Geary cable ran for the last time on 5 May 1912 [2].

Construction had crawled under Mayor P. H. McCarthy. His successor, James Rolph, brought in the traction expert Bion J. Arnold and moved to contract building. The remaining 3.5 miles of track were finished in less than six months [1]. The builder W. L. Holman had delivered only 10 of the 43 cars ordered [3]. Rolph drove the first car himself and told the crowd: 'It is in reality the people's road, built by the people and with the people's money' [2]. The sources give the opening date as 28 December or 30 December 1912 [2][3]. Supporters called it the nation's first municipally owned streetcar line [1].

title: A cathedral for selling Packards

place.label: Earle C. Anthony Packard Showroom, 901 Van Ness Avenue at Ellis

hook: On Auto Row, Bernard Maybeck built a car showroom from Numidian marble and Persian lanterns and told his workmen to imagine a medieval cathedral.
story:
By the mid-1920s the new-car trade had settled along Van Ness Avenue [1]. Earle C. Anthony was, according to Wikipedia, the world's most prominent Packard dealer, selling one of every seven Packards between 1915 and 1957. He also founded the Los Angeles radio station KFI [2]. For his San Francisco showroom at Van Ness and Ellis he hired Bernard Maybeck, the architect of the Palace of Fine Arts [4]. Sources date the building to 1926 or 1927 [3][4].

The opening night drew Hollywood starlets and was broadcast on one of Anthony's radio stations [3]. His booklet 'A Saga of Transportation' described rose marble from Numidia and black marble from Belgium, travertine, scagliola, 'lanterns from a Persian Hareem', and Spanish and Gothic doorways, which together made 'an Aladdin's palace' [3]. The booklet also printed Maybeck's instructions to the builders: 'Imagine that no cars roar by on Van Ness Avenue and that no telephone will call you from your work. Believe yourselves, instead, working in the gloom of a cathedral of the Middle Ages' [3].

title: Julia Morgan's clubhouse hosts the Supreme Court

place.label: Century Club of California, 1355 Franklin Street

hook: A women's club hired one of its own members, a young architect named Julia Morgan. After the fire, the state's highest court moved into the clubhouse.
story:
The Century Club of California was founded in 1888 as a private women's club [1]. Its early officers included Sarah B. Cooper, who founded the Golden Gate Kindergarten Association, a network of 50 kindergartens, served on the board of the Associated Charities and later turned to women's suffrage. She was the club's vice-president [2].

For its Franklin Street clubhouse, completed in 1905, the club chose one of its members, Julia Morgan [1]. She had recently returned from the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. In 1904 she became the first woman licensed as an architect in California and opened her San Francisco practice, so the clubhouse was one of her first commissions [1][3].

The clubhouse survived the earthquake and fire of April 1906. Afterwards it temporarily housed the California State Supreme Court [1]. Morgan's own office had burned [3]. She was then chosen to redesign the fire-gutted Fairmont Hotel because she had a rare knowledge of earthquake-resistant reinforced concrete [3].

title: Maybeck builds for the city's charity

place.label: Family Service Agency (Associated Charities) building, 1010 Gough Street at Eddy

hook: Bernard Maybeck designed a Mediterranean home for the Associated Charities. Across the street stood a mansion that would later appear in Vertigo.
story:
The Associated Charities of San Francisco dates to 1889 [1]. The kindergarten pioneer Sarah B. Cooper was one of its directors [2]. In 1928 Bernard Maybeck designed a Mediterranean-style headquarters for the organisation at Gough and Eddy. In 1938 it renamed itself the Family Service Agency, partly to escape the stigma attached to the word 'charity' [1].

When the building was new, most of its neighbours were fine Italianate row houses. Next door was the 1880 Hugo Rothschild House, which became a rooming house early in its life [1][3]. The corner was shared with St. Paulus Lutheran Church and the twenty-room mansion Henry F. Fortmann built in 1888 at 1007 Gough [1]. The Call reported that on 26 February 1901 Emma Fortmann married Dr. W. E. Stevens at the house [1]. The mansion was demolished in 1959, a year after it played the McKittrick Hotel in Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo. Many websites wrongly call it the 'Portman' mansion [1]. The Rothschild house has since been restored as a single-family home [3].
